nodes.name: Show on a number line that a number plus its opposite is 0
nodes.statement: On a number line, starting at a and moving |a| in the direction of -a, back toward 0, lands exactly on 0, so a + (-a) = 0.
nodes.assess: Use a number line to show why 3.5 + (-3.5) = 0.

proposed_edges.rationale: The explanation starts at a and moves |a| along the number line, which is the move that the sum a + (-a) means.
The test problem places 3.5 and -3.5 on a number line before moving 3.5 units back to 0.
The statement moves in the direction of -a back toward 0, using that -a lies on the other side of 0 at the same distance as a.

nodes.name: Describe a real-world situation for a sum of signed numbers
nodes.statement: Describe a real-world situation that a given sum of rational numbers represents, giving each addend a meaning in the situation.
nodes.assess: Describe a real-world situation that the sum -12 + 4.5 could represent.

proposed_edges.rationale: The situation must show the sum as a starting value followed by a change, which is the move of |q| from p that the number line gives.
Each addend, such as -12, needs a meaning in the situation, so the writer must know that a negative number names the opposite direction from 0.

nodes.name: Add two integers
nodes.statement: Add two integers by the sign rules: with the same sign, add the absolute values and keep the sign; with opposite signs, subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger and take the sign of the addend with the larger absolute value.
procedure: If one addend is 0, the sum is the other addend.
If the addends have the same sign, add their absolute values and give the sum that sign.

If they have opposite signs, subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger and give the result the sign of the addend with the larger absolute value; if the absolute values are equal, the sum is 0.

proposed_edges.rationale: Steps 2 and 3 add or subtract the absolute values of the addends, which are the distances of -6 and -8 from 0.
Step 2 adds the absolute values of two same-sign addends, such as 6 + 8, and any method for that sum will do.
Step 2 adds two absolute values, which are whole numbers, and any method for the sum will do.
Step 3 must decide which addend has the larger absolute value, which means deciding which of two whole numbers is greater.
Step 3 first decides which absolute value is larger, to know what to subtract and whose sign to keep.
The sign rules compute the sum of signed numbers, which is defined as a move along the number line.
Step 3 says the sum is 0 when the absolute values are equal, as in 7 + (-7), because opposites are additive inverses.
The sign rules refer to whether each addend is positive or negative, so the meaning of the sign of an integer is used throughout.
Step 3 subtracts the smaller absolute value from the larger, such as 9 - 4, and any method for that difference will do.
Step 3 subtracts the smaller absolute value from the larger, a whole-number difference by any method.

nodes.name: Add two signed fractions or decimals
nodes.statement: Add two rational numbers given as signed fractions or decimals by the sign rules for addition, computing the sum or difference of their absolute values as fractions or decimals.
procedure: If one addend is 0, the sum is the other addend.
If the addends have the same sign, add their absolute values as fractions or decimals and give the sum that sign.

If they have opposite signs, subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger as fractions or decimals and give the result the sign of the addend with the larger absolute value; if the absolute values are equal, the sum is 0.

proposed_edges.rationale: Steps 2 and 3 work with the absolute values of fraction and decimal addends such as 2.4 and 1/2.
Step 2 adds absolute values given as decimals, and the decimal points must be lined up in the sum.
Step 3 decides which decimal addend has the larger absolute value, such as 2.4 against 0.75, to choose the sign.
Step 3 subtracts decimal absolute values, such as 2.4 - 0.75, which have different numbers of decimal places.
Step 2 adds absolute values given as fractions, as in 1/2 + 1/3, and the denominators may differ.
Step 3 must decide which fraction absolute value is larger to know what to subtract and which sign to keep.
Step 3 decides which fraction addend has the larger absolute value when the addends have opposite signs.
Step 3 subtracts the smaller absolute value from the larger when these are fractions with different denominators.
The statement adds rational numbers by the sign rules for addition, which the integer node states and this node applies to fractions and decimals.

nodes.name: Subtracting a number is adding its opposite
nodes.statement: For all rational numbers p and q, p - q = p + (-q).
nodes.assess: Which expressions equal 5 - (-8): 5 + 8; 5 + (-8); -5 + 8? Which equal -3 - 7: -3 + (-7); -3 + 7?

proposed_edges.rationale: The sum p + (-q) with a negative second addend is meant as a move along the number line.
The right side p + (-q) is a sum of signed rational numbers, so the meaning and value of such sums is used.
Showing that p - q equals p + (-q) uses that q + (-q) = 0, so -q is the additive inverse of q.
The test problem asks about 5 - (-8), where -q is -(-8), so the learner must know the opposite of -8 is 8.

nodes.name: Subtract two integers
nodes.statement: Subtract one integer from another by rewriting the subtraction as adding the opposite and adding the two integers.
procedure: Rewrite p - q as p + (-q).
Add p and -q by the sign rules for adding integers.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 2 adds p and -q by the sign rules for adding integers.
Step 1 produces -q, and when q is negative, as in -5 - (-9), the result -(-9) must be seen as 9.
Step 1 rewrites p - q as p + (-q), which is exactly the identity that the add-the-opposite concept states.

nodes.name: Subtract two signed fractions or decimals
nodes.statement: Subtract one rational number given as a signed fraction or decimal from another by rewriting the subtraction as adding the opposite and adding the two numbers.

Add p and -q by the sign rules for adding signed fractions or decimals.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 2 adds p and -q by the sign rules for adding signed fractions or decimals.
Step 1 produces -q, and for 1/4 - (-2/3) the result -(-2/3) must be seen as 2/3.
Step 1 rewrites p - q as p + (-q), which is exactly the identity that the add-the-opposite concept states.

nodes.name: The distance between two numbers is the absolute value of their difference
nodes.statement: The distance between two rational numbers p and q on the number line is |p - q|, which equals |q - p|.
nodes.assess: Which expressions give the distance between -6 and 2 on the number line: |-6 - 2|; |-6 + 2|; |2 - (-6)|; -6 - 2?

nodes.name: Show on a number line that distance is the absolute value of the difference
nodes.statement: For a specific pair of rational numbers, a number line shows that the distance between them equals the absolute value of their difference, taken in either order.
nodes.assess: Use a number line to show that the distance between -3 and 5 equals |5 - (-3)| and also |-3 - 5|.

The difference p - q is read as the amount to add to q to land on p, in either order.

nodes.name: Solve real-world problems about how far apart two signed values are
nodes.statement: A real-world problem gives two signed values of the same kind, such as two elevations, temperatures or balances, and asks how far apart they are, answered by the absolute value of their difference.

nodes.name: Add signed numbers by reordering and regrouping
nodes.statement: Add several rational numbers by using the commutative and associative properties of addition to reorder and regroup them so that opposites, or addends with an easy sum, are combined first.
nodes.assess: Compute -3.7 + 8 + 3.7 by first reordering and grouping the addends. Show the rewritten sum.

nodes.statement: Compute an expression that subtracts rational numbers by rewriting each subtraction as adding the opposite, then reordering and regrouping the addends with the commutative and associative properties of addition.

Add each group, then add the results.

Step 1 rewrites each p - q as p + (-q), the identity that the add-the-opposite concept states.

nodes.name: Solve real-world problems that add a signed change to a signed value
nodes.statement: A real-world problem gives a signed starting value and a signed change, such as an elevation and a rise or fall, and asks for the result, found by adding the two signed numbers.
nodes.assess: A submarine is at -45.5 m. It rises 18.25 m. What is its new elevation?

proposed_edges.rationale: The result is found by adding a signed starting value and a signed change, such as -45.5 and 18.25.
The change is given as a rise or fall, so the learner must write a fall as a negative number and a rise as a positive one.
A rise or fall in the story must be written as a positive or negative change before it is added.

nodes.name: Solve real-world problems that find the signed change between two values
nodes.statement: A real-world problem gives two signed values of the same kind, such as two temperatures or elevations, and asks for the change from the first to the second, found by subtracting the first from the second.
nodes.assess: At noon the temperature was 4.5 degrees C. At midnight it was -7.25 degrees C. What was the change in temperature from noon to midnight?

proposed_edges.rationale: The answer is a signed change, and a negative result must be read as a decrease in temperature.
The change is found by subtracting the first value from the second, such as 4.5 from -7.25.
The change from the first value to the second is the amount added to the first to reach the second, so second minus first.

nodes.name: The sign rule for multiplying signed numbers
nodes.statement: The product of two nonzero rational numbers is positive when they have the same sign and negative when they have opposite signs, and its absolute value is the product of their absolute values.
nodes.assess: Without computing the values, give the sign of each product: (-3.1) x 4.7; (-2/5) x (-8); 0.5 x 12.

proposed_edges.rationale: The rule states that the absolute value of the product is the product of the absolute values of the factors.
The product of the absolute values is an ordinary product of nonnegative decimals, as in 3.1 x 4.7.
The product of the absolute values is an ordinary product of nonnegative fractions or whole numbers.
The rule sorts factors by whether they have the same sign or opposite signs, so the sign of a number must be meaningful.

nodes.name: Explain with the distributive property why (-1) x (-1) = 1
nodes.statement: If multiplication of signed numbers keeps the distributive property, then 0 = (-1) x (1 + (-1)) = (-1) x 1 + (-1) x (-1) = -1 + (-1) x (-1), so (-1) x (-1) must be the additive inverse of -1, which is 1.
nodes.assess: Use 0 = (-1) x (1 + (-1)) and the distributive property to explain why (-1) x (-1) must equal 1.

proposed_edges.rationale: The argument replaces (-1) x 1 by -1, which uses that multiplying by 1 leaves a number unchanged.
The first step uses that (-1) times 0 is 0, which is why the left side of the chain equals 0.
The argument splits (-1) x (1 + (-1)) into (-1) x 1 + (-1) x (-1) by the distributive property.
The argument uses 1 + (-1) = 0 and concludes that (-1) x (-1) is the additive inverse of -1.

nodes.name: Multiply two integers
nodes.statement: Multiply two integers by multiplying their absolute values and giving the product the sign from the sign rule.
nodes.assess: Compute -6 x 7, -4 x (-9), and 0 x (-3).
procedure: If either factor is 0, the product is 0.
Multiply the absolute values of the factors.
Make the product positive if the factors have the same sign and negative if they have opposite signs.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 2 multiplies the absolute values of the factors, so each integer must be read as its distance from 0.
Step 2 multiplies two whole numbers, the absolute values, and any method for the product will do.
Step 1 says the product is 0 if either factor is 0, as in 0 x (-3).
Step 2 multiplies absolute values such as 6 and 7, and recalled facts or any other method will do.

nodes.name: Multiply two signed fractions or decimals

procedure: If either factor is 0, the product is 0.

nodes.name: Describe a real-world situation for a product of signed numbers

The factor -2.5 needs a meaning in the situation, so the writer must know what a negative quantity describes.

nodes.name: A quotient of integers is a rational number
nodes.statement: For integers p and q with q not 0, p divided by q is the rational number p/q, even when q does not divide p evenly.
nodes.assess: Write (-7) divided by 2 as a fraction. Which of these quotients is a rational number and which is undefined: 0 divided by (-3); 4 divided by 0?

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement requires q not 0, and the test problem asks which quotient is undefined, such as 4 divided by 0.
Dividing integers, including negative ones, means finding the factor that multiplies the divisor to give the dividend, as for (-7) divided by 2.
The statement says p divided by q is the fraction p/q, which extends a divided by b equals a/b from whole numbers to integers.
A quotient such as (-7) divided by 2 is a fraction with a negative numerator, a point left of 0 on the number line.

nodes.name: The sign rule for dividing signed numbers
nodes.statement: The quotient of two nonzero rational numbers is positive when they have the same sign and negative when they have opposite signs, and its absolute value is the quotient of their absolute values.
nodes.assess: Without computing the values, give the sign of each quotient: (-48) divided by 6; (-2.4) divided by (-0.8); (5/6) divided by (-3).

proposed_edges.rationale: The rule states that the absolute value of the quotient is the quotient of the absolute values of the two numbers.
The quotient of the absolute values is an ordinary quotient of nonnegative decimals, as in 2.4 divided by 0.8.
A quotient is the factor that multiplies the divisor to give the dividend, which links the division signs to the multiplication signs.
The quotient of the absolute values is an ordinary quotient of nonnegative fractions or whole numbers.
The sign of the quotient is the sign that makes quotient times divisor equal the dividend under the multiplication sign rule.

nodes.name: Where the negative sign of a fraction can go
nodes.statement: For integers p and q with q not 0, -(p/q) = (-p)/q = p/(-q).

proposed_edges.rationale: Moving the negative sign between numerator, denominator and front uses the sign of a quotient of a negative by a positive and a positive by a negative.
The fractions p/q, (-p)/q and p/(-q) have integer numerators and denominators, so each is a quotient of integers.
The expression -(p/q) is the opposite of a fraction, so the meaning of the opposite of a number is used.

nodes.name: Divide an integer by an integer that divides it evenly
nodes.statement: Divide an integer by a nonzero integer that divides it evenly by dividing their absolute values and giving the quotient the sign from the sign rule.
nodes.assess: Compute -42 divided by 6, -36 divided by (-4), and 0 divided by (-5).
procedure: If the dividend is 0, the quotient is 0.
Divide the absolute value of the dividend by the absolute value of the divisor.
Make the quotient positive if the two numbers have the same sign and negative if they have opposite signs.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 2 divides the absolute values of the two integers, so each must be read as its distance from 0.
Step 2 divides one whole number by another that divides it evenly, and any method will do.
Step 2 divides absolute values such as 42 by 6, which are recalled division facts, and the zero dividend case follows from them.
Step 3 gives the quotient its sign by the rule for same signs and opposite signs.

nodes.name: Divide signed fractions or decimals
nodes.statement: Divide a rational number by a nonzero rational number, given as signed fractions or decimals, by dividing their absolute values as fractions or decimals and giving the quotient the sign from the sign rule.
nodes.assess: Compute -1.8 divided by 0.3 and (-2/3) divided by (-4/5).
procedure: If the dividend is 0, the quotient is 0.
Divide the absolute value of the dividend by the absolute value of the divisor as fractions or decimals.
Make the quotient positive if the two numbers have the same sign and negative if they have opposite signs.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 2 divides the absolute values of the two numbers, so each fraction or decimal must be read as its distance from 0.
Step 2 divides decimal absolute values such as 1.8 by 0.3, which needs division by a decimal.
Step 2 divides fraction absolute values such as 2/3 by 4/5.
Step 3 gives the quotient its sign by the rule for same signs and opposite signs.

nodes.name: Describe a real-world situation for a quotient of signed numbers
nodes.statement: Describe a real-world situation that a given quotient of rational numbers represents, giving the dividend and the divisor a meaning in the situation.

nodes.statement: Multiply rational numbers by using the commutative and associative properties to reorder and regroup factors, or the distributive property to split a factor into a sum, so that the products are easy.

nodes.name: Divide signed numbers by rewriting as multiplication and regrouping
nodes.statement: Compute an expression that divides rational numbers by rewriting each division as multiplying by the reciprocal of the divisor, then reordering and regrouping the factors with the commutative and associative properties.
nodes.assess: Compute [(-18) divided by (2/3)] x (1/9) by rewriting the division as a multiplication and regrouping. Show the rewritten product.

Multiply each group, then multiply the results.

Step 2 moves and groups factors with the commutative and associative properties of multiplication.

nodes.name: Solve real-world problems that multiply a signed change per unit
nodes.statement: A real-world problem gives a constant signed change per unit, such as per day or per hour, and a number of units, and asks for the total change, found by multiplying.

nodes.statement: A real-world problem gives a total signed change spread equally over a number of steps or units and asks for the change per step, found by dividing.

proposed_edges.rationale: The total is spread equally over the steps, which is the sharing meaning of a quotient.
The change per step is found by dividing a total signed change by a number of steps, such as -22.5 by 5.
The total change is signed, so a descent in elevation must be written and read as a negative number.

nodes.name: Convert a fraction to a decimal with long division
nodes.statement: Write a fraction a/b of whole numbers as a decimal by dividing a by b with long division, writing zeros after the decimal point of a, until a remainder of 0 ends the decimal or a remainder recurs, after which the digits repeat.

procedure: Write a with a decimal point and zeros after it, and set up a divided by b.
Divide with long division, placing the decimal point of the quotient above that of a.
If a remainder is 0, stop: the decimal terminates.
If a remainder appears that has appeared before, stop: the quotient digits from where that remainder first appeared repeat forever; record the repeating block.

Steps 3 and 4 watch each remainder, stopping at a remainder of 0 or at one seen before, so what a remainder is must be known.

nodes.name: The decimal form of a rational number terminates or eventually repeats
nodes.statement: The decimal form of a rational number either terminates, ending in 0s, or eventually repeats one block of digits forever.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement is about the decimal form of a rational number, which is a number written as a quotient of integers.

proposed_edges.rationale: After the conversion, the two decimal quantities, such as 0.625 and 0.6, are compared to decide which is greater.
The fraction quantity, such as 5/8, is converted to a decimal by long division before the comparison.

nodes.name: A rational number is a quotient of integers
nodes.statement: A rational number is a number that can be written as p/q for some integers p and q with q not 0.
nodes.assess: Show that -1.25, 3 1/2 and 6 are rational numbers by writing each as a quotient of two integers.

proposed_edges.rationale: The test problem writes -1.25 as a quotient of integers, which uses reading 1.25 as 125 hundredths.
The test problem writes the mixed number 3 1/2 as the quotient 7/2.
The test problem writes the whole number 6 as a quotient of integers, 6/1.
The definition says a rational number is p/q for integers p and q, which is the quotient of integers that this concept names.
Writing -1.25 as (-125)/100 puts the negative sign in the numerator, as the sign placement identity allows.

nodes.name: Explain why the decimal of a fraction terminates or repeats
nodes.statement: In the long division of a whole number a by a positive whole number b, every remainder is one of 0, 1, ..., b - 1, and once the digits of a are used up each step depends only on the remainder; so within b such steps either a remainder is 0 and the decimal terminates, or a remainder recurs and from then on the digits repeat.
nodes.assess: When you divide 1 by 7 with long division, explain why some remainder must recur within 7 steps after the decimal point, and why the digits of the quotient repeat from then on.

proposed_edges.rationale: The argument lists the possible remainders 0, 1, ..., b - 1, which are the remainders smaller than the divisor b.
Only b remainders are possible, so within b steps either 0 appears or some remainder must come up a second time.
The argument concludes that a remainder must recur within b steps because only b different remainders exist.
The argument is about the steps of the long division of a by b, each step depending on the remainder before it.

nodes.name: Write an eventually repeating decimal as a quotient of integers
nodes.statement: Write an eventually repeating decimal x as a quotient of integers by subtracting x from 10^k x, where k is the number of digits in the repeating block, so that the repeating parts cancel, and solving for x.
nodes.assess: Write 0.8333..., with the 3 repeating, as a quotient of two integers.
procedure: Let x be the decimal and k the number of digits in its repeating block.
Write 10^k x by moving the decimal point of x k places to the right.
Subtract x from 10^k x; the repeating parts cancel, leaving (10^k - 1) x = d, where d is a terminating decimal.
Write x = d/(10^k - 1), and multiply the numerator and denominator by a power of 10 if needed so both are integers.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 3 subtracts x from 10^k x as decimals so that the repeating parts cancel and a terminating decimal d remains.
Step 4 solves (10^k - 1) x = d for x by dividing both sides by 10^k - 1.
Step 2 writes the multiplier as 10^k, a power of 10 with a whole-number exponent.
Step 3 combines 10^k x - x as (10^k - 1) x, the like terms in x.
The decimal is named x, a letter standing for one number, so that 10^k x and x can be subtracted.
Step 4 multiplies the numerator and denominator by a power of 10 to clear the decimal, producing an equivalent fraction.
Step 4 writes the solution x as the fraction d/(10^k - 1), a division written as a fraction.

nodes.name: Every number has a decimal expansion
nodes.statement: Every number on the number line has a decimal expansion, possibly never ending, whose digits record which tenth, then which hundredth, and so on, the number lies in.
nodes.assess: A point P on the number line lies between 0.7 and 0.8, and between 0.73 and 0.74. What are the first two digits after the decimal point in the decimal expansion of P?

nodes.name: An irrational number is a number that is not rational
nodes.statement: A number that cannot be written as p/q with integers p and q and q not 0 is called irrational.
nodes.assess: Which of these are irrational: 0.25, which equals 1/4; sqrt(2), which cannot be written as a quotient of integers; -7; 0.333..., which equals 1/3?

nodes.name: Classify a number as rational or irrational
nodes.statement: Classify a number given in one of these forms: integers, fractions of integers, terminating decimals, eventually repeating decimals and square roots of perfect squares are rational; square roots of whole numbers that are not perfect squares, pi, and decimals that neither terminate nor repeat are irrational.
nodes.assess: Classify each as rational or irrational: sqrt(16); sqrt(15); 0.121212... with 12 repeating; 0.1211211121111... with one more 1 each time; pi; -4/9.
procedure: If the number is an integer, a fraction of integers, or a terminating or eventually repeating decimal, it is rational.
If it is the square root of a whole number, it is rational when that whole number is a perfect square and irrational otherwise.
If it is pi, or a decimal that neither terminates nor repeats, it is irrational.

nodes.name: Bound a number between truncations of its decimal expansion
nodes.statement: If t is the decimal expansion of a positive number x cut off after n decimal places, then t <= x <= t + 1/10^n, which bounds x between two decimals with n places.
nodes.assess: pi = 3.14159... Between which two consecutive hundredths does pi lie?
procedure: Cut off the decimal expansion of x after n decimal places to get t.
Add 1 in the last place kept to get t + 1/10^n.
State that x lies between t and t + 1/10^n.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 2 adds 1 in the last place kept to t, a decimal addition that can carry, as in 3.149 + 0.001.

nodes.name: Find decimal bounds for a square root by squaring
nodes.statement: Find decimals with a given number of places between which sqrt(n) lies, for a whole number n that is not a perfect square, by squaring trial values: first consecutive whole numbers, then consecutive tenths, then consecutive hundredths.
nodes.assess: Without a calculator, show that sqrt(5) is between 2 and 3, and then between 2.2 and 2.3.
procedure: Find the whole number a with a^2 < n < (a + 1)^2.
Square a + 0.1, a + 0.2, and so on, until a square first exceeds n; sqrt(n) lies between that value and the one before it.
Repeat inside that interval with steps of 0.01, and so on, for each further decimal place.

nodes.name: Compare irrational numbers with decimal bounds

nodes.assess: Which is greater, sqrt(10) or pi? Use decimal bounds for each to decide.
procedure: Bound each number between two consecutive tenths.
If the two intervals overlap, bound each between consecutive hundredths, and so on, until they do not overlap.
The number whose interval lies to the right is the greater.
